title: Spiking Neural Networks: The Future of Brain-Inspired Computing
venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology
tldr: A unified multi-metric comparison of three SNN training paradigms demonstrates that surrogate gradient methods achieve near-ANN accuracy with 10 ms latency, while STDP-based models consume only 5 mJ per inference.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional ANNs achieve high classification accuracy but are extremely energy inefficient and lack biological realism. Most existing SNN studies evaluate a single training paradigm or a single metric in isolation, obscuring practical tradeoffs for deployment-oriented model selection.
approach: Evaluated three SNN training paradigms - surrogate gradient descent, ANN-to-SNN conversion, and STDP - under a unified protocol across five performance metrics.
Used MNIST, CIFAR-10, DVS128 Gesture, and SHD/SSC datasets covering both static and neuromorphic input conditions.
Simulated SNNs using Brian2 for surrogate gradient models, BindsNET for conversion pipelines, and NEST for large-scale spiking models.
Applied the LIF neuron model with membrane time constant 20 ms, threshold voltage 1.0, and refractory period 5 ms.
Evaluated performance across accuracy, latency, energy consumption, spike count, and convergence behavior over 20 training epochs.
Used NVIDIA RTX GPU workstation with 32 GB RAM for training, ensuring comparability with prior benchmarks.
Compared SNN results against ANN (CNN) baselines to quantify relative improvements in energy efficiency and latency.
Reported mean and standard deviation across five independent runs with varying random seeds for statistical robustness.
findings: Surrogate gradient SNNs achieved 97.8% +/- 0.2 accuracy on MNIST, within 1-2% of ANN baselines.
Converted SNNs achieved 98.1% +/- 0.3 on MNIST and 89.3% +/- 0.4 on CIFAR-10.
STDP-based SNNs achieved 95.5% +/- 0.4 on MNIST and 74.2% +/- 0.6 on CIFAR-10.
Surrogate gradient SNNs achieved 10 ms inference latency compared to 45 ms for ANN (CNN) baselines.
STDP-based SNNs consumed only 5 mJ per inference with approximately 4,000 spikes, compared to 200 mJ for ANNs.
Surrogate gradient SNNs reduced training loss from 0.9 to 0.44 over 20 epochs, fastest among all models.
SNNs achieve 90-97% energy savings relative to ANNs while maintaining competitive accuracy.
Converted SNNs reduce energy consumption by approximately 90% compared to ANN counterparts.
No single SNN model dominates all performance dimensions; optimal choice depends on application priorities.
Hardware standardization and scalable training remain significant obstacles for broad SNN adoption.
key_figures_tables: Table 1: SNN performance summary across MNIST and CIFAR-10 -> ANN leads accuracy but STDP leads efficiency.
Table 2: Latency comparison across models -> Surrogate gradient SNNs achieve lowest 10 ms latency.
Table 3: Energy efficiency and spike count per inference -> STDP consumes 5 mJ with fewest spikes.
Figure 3: Accuracy vs energy tradeoffs across models -> SNNs achieve 90-97% energy savings with marginal accuracy loss.
Figure 4: Latency comparison across models -> SNNs 2-3x faster than ANNs in inference.
Figure 5: Energy and spike count per inference -> STDP most efficient, ANN most expensive.
Figure 6: Training loss convergence over 20 epochs -> Surrogate gradient SNNs converge fastest.
Figure 7: Learning curves showing training accuracy -> Surrogate gradient SNNs stabilize near 98%.

key_equations.equation: Accuracy = Number of Correct Predictions / Total Number of Predictions * 100%
key_equations.explanation: Standard classification accuracy metric for SNN evaluation.
Time from input stimulus to first output neuron spike.

key_equations.equation: Total Spikes = sum over t and i of s_i(t)
key_equations.explanation: Aggregate spike count measuring computational sparsity.
Total energy from spike and synaptic operations combined.

key_equations.equation: Convergence Time = Epoch_min where Accuracy_epoch >= Target Accuracy
key_equations.explanation: Minimum epochs required to reach target accuracy.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a unified, multi-metric comparative analysis of three principal SNN training paradigms - surrogate gradient descent, ANN-to-SNN conversion, and STDP - under a consistent evaluation protocol.
directly_justifies: Surrogate gradient SNNs achieve 97.8% accuracy on MNIST with only 10 ms inference latency.
STDP-based SNNs consume as low as 5 mJ per inference with approximately 4,000 spikes.
SNNs achieve 90-97% energy savings relative to ANNs with only 1-3% accuracy loss.
Converted SNNs reduce energy consumption by approximately 90% while preserving ANN-level accuracy.
No single SNN paradigm dominates all performance axes; suitability depends on application requirements.
limits: Evaluation relies primarily on benchmark datasets that may not capture real-world deployment complexity.
Hardware-specific results drawn from reported benchmarks rather than direct implementation in this study.
Hyperparameter sensitivity in surrogate-gradient training and convergence instability in STDP require further exploration.
Scalability on high-dimensional tasks and robustness under noisy conditions remain unaddressed.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. The paper is primarily about Spiking Neural Networks and neuromorphic computing, which falls outside the personal finance focus. Domain 6 was flagged as contextual because SNNs are a class of predictive model for sequential data, though not applied to finance. Domain 14 was flagged as contextual because the paper extensively discusses SNN deployment on neuromorphic and edge hardware and on-device vs. cloud inference tradeoffs. All personal finance domains (1-5, 7, 10-13) were considered and rejected.

limitations: Evaluation relies primarily on benchmark datasets that may not fully capture real-world complexity or large-scale deployment scenarios.
Hardware-specific results are drawn from reported benchmarks in the literature rather than from direct implementation in this study.
Hyperparameter sensitivity in surrogate-gradient training and convergence instability in STDP highlight ongoing challenges.
Scalability on high-dimensional tasks and robustness under noisy conditions remain areas for future research.
